title: The Historian Who Became a Geometer: Baltimore, Princeton, and the Only Fields Medal Given to a Physicist
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Baltimore, a Boyhood Not Pointed at Physics

stops.name: Baltimore, the birth in a physicist's house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate is the canonical Baltimore pin inherited byte-identical from edgar_allan_poe.journey.json
stops.campa: A son is born on the twenty-sixth of August to Louis and Lorraine Witten, in a Baltimore of brick rows and white marble steps. The father is a theoretical physicist working on gravitation, so the child grows up in a house where general relativity is ordinary table talk, equations at the dinner table before he has any way to judge whether that is unusual. There are four children in that house: Edward, Celia, Matthew, Jesse. Which of them comes first is nowhere recorded.
suggested_refs: Louis Witten's published work on general relativity, the household trade Edward Witten did not at first take up

stops.name: Israel, the year the family lives abroad
stops.date_confidence: decade only. Wikipedia says the family lived in Israel for one year during the 1960s and names neither the year nor the city; 1960 is a default and the Jerusalem coordinate is a placeholder for the whole country, deliberately not the atlas's Temple Mount pin
stops.campa: For one year in the nineteen-sixties the family lives in Israel. No source names the city, no source names the year, and the pin on this map is Jerusalem standing in for a whole country. The boy is somewhere between eight and seventeen; he comes back to Baltimore and finishes school there. Nothing in the record says what the year did to him, and nothing says it did anything at all. It is the one stretch of his childhood spent outside the United States, and it is the emptiest entry in his biography.
suggested_refs: The unlocated Israeli year, a gap in every published biography of Witten

stops.name: Johns Hopkins, the colloquium a boy of fifteen does not attend
stops.date_confidence: 18 October 1966 attested for the colloquium, recorded identically in four existing corpus journeys; Witten's residence in Baltimore that year follows from his birth and schooling, and no source places him in the building
stops.campa: At fifteen he is an ordinary student in a Baltimore day school, two years from the graduation that will send him toward journalism and politics rather than the family trade. Nothing in any source marks this particular year as a turning point: no prize, no mentor, no early paper. What is on record is only where he lives and how old he is, a boy with a physicist father and no stated interest yet in physics, eight years still ahead of the subject that will define him.
suggested_refs: Witten's own account of his pre-physics interests in journalism and politics, in interviews given decades later

stops.name: Park School of Baltimore, the graduation
stops.date_confidence: 1968 attested; the month is conventional. The coordinate is corrected from the gathering pass, which was about 1.4 km off; the school has stood on the Old Court Road campus since 1959
stops.campa: He graduates in 1968 from the Park School of Baltimore, out on Old Court Road, where the school has stood since 1959. Nothing in the record marks him as a boy pointed at physics. There is no science fair and no mathematics olympiad, and the subject Louis Witten practices for a living is one his son has not taken up. What he wants at seventeen is journalism and politics. He leaves for Brandeis to read history, and the physics waits eight more years for him.
suggested_refs: Park School of Baltimore, 2425 Old Court Road, the campus occupied since 1959

segments.name: History, Linguistics, and a Losing Campaign

stops.name: New York, the political journalism of an undergraduate
stops.date_confidence: late 1960s per Wikipedia; no year and no composition city are sourced. The Nation was published from New York and The New Republic from Washington, D.C., so this pin is a placeholder that is at best half right. The gathering pass dated these pieces to 1972, which the source does not support
stops.campa: Before he is out of college he is publishing: political pieces in The New Republic and in The Nation, written by an undergraduate who intends to make his living this way. Which desk in which city he wrote them at is not recorded. The Nation is a New York paper and The New Republic a Washington one, so the pin here is a convenience and not an address. He is nineteen or twenty, and the trade he is training for is opinion. Nothing he prints in these years has anything to do with gauge fields.
suggested_refs: Witten's late-1960s contributions to The New Republic and The Nation, uncollected and unindexed

stops.name: Brandeis University, the degree in history
stops.date_confidence: the 1971 bachelor's degree is attested; the month is conventional for a commencement
stops.campa: He takes the bachelor's degree at Brandeis in Waltham in 1971: a major in history, a minor in linguistics, and no physics and no mathematics anywhere on the transcript. What he studies is how societies argue and how languages hold together. Nineteen years on, the Fields Medal citation will say that his command of mathematics is rivalled by few mathematicians. At the moment he leaves Waltham he has not taken a graduate course in the subject and has no plan to take one.
suggested_refs: Brandeis University, which gave Witten his first degree in 1971 and an honorary one in 1988

stops.name: Washington, six months on the McGovern campaign
stops.date_confidence: 1972 and the six-month duration are attested; no office, city, or posting within the campaign is named in any source, so Washington is a placeholder and the month is defaulted
stops.campa: He goes to work for George McGovern, six months as a staffer on a presidential campaign that will carry one state and the District of Columbia. Which office, which city, which job inside the machine, none of it is written down. He is twenty-one and the country is arguing about a war. When the campaign ends he is out of a trade: the journalism has not become a career and the politics has just lost by the widest margin of the century. He enrolls in economics at Michigan instead.
suggested_refs: The 1972 McGovern presidential campaign, on whose staff Witten served roughly six months

stops.name: Ann Arbor, the economics he abandons
stops.date_confidence: 1972 attested for the enrollment and the withdrawal; no duration is given beyond the word briefly, and the month is conventional for an academic year
stops.campa: Ann Arbor takes him as a graduate student in economics, and he leaves without finishing. The record gives no reason and no length of stay beyond the word briefly. In three years he has been a historian, a journalist, a campaign staffer and an economist, and none of the four has held. Then he applies to Princeton in applied mathematics, a field he has not studied, at twenty-two, holding a degree in the humanities and no record of study in the sciences at all.
suggested_refs: University of Michigan graduate economics program, entered and left in 1972

segments.name: The Turn: Princeton and the Doctorate

stops.name: Princeton University, enrolling in applied mathematics
stops.date_confidence: 1973 attested for the enrollment; the month is conventional for the start of an academic year
stops.campa: Princeton admits him to applied mathematics and he shifts almost at once into physics, which is where he stays. He is starting behind every classmate in the department and will not stay behind any of them for long. David Gross takes him on. The problem set in front of him is the short-distance behaviour of gauge theories, the deep structure of the quantum field theory that was assembled while he was reading history at Brandeis. He is twenty-two and four years from a doctorate.
suggested_refs: Princeton University graduate school records for the 1973 entering cohort

stops.name: Green Bank, the summer at the radio telescopes
stops.date_confidence: 1974 attested for the NRAO summer studentship; Wikipedia names the observatory but not the site, and Green Bank is a reconstruction from where the summer program historically ran. The month is conventional
stops.campa: For a summer he is a student at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, in the radio-quiet zone of West Virginia where petrol engines and microwave ovens are regulated so the dishes can hear. Which of the observatory's sites took him is not stated in the sources, and Green Bank is the reconstruction, since that is where the summer program ran. It is the only observational work in a life spent otherwise at blackboards, and nothing in the later career refers back to it.
suggested_refs: The NRAO summer student program and the National Radio Quiet Zone, Green Bank, West Virginia

stops.name: Jones Hall, the address the department left behind
stops.date_confidence: no date attested and no event. The pin is the old Fine Hall coordinate inherited byte-identical from dirac.journey.json; Witten's department had moved to Jadwin Hall in 1970 and no source places him in this building. The date is a convention for the middle of his doctorate
stops.campa: The department he is in has moved, in 1970, into Jadwin Hall. Its older address stands a few hundred yards away: the building called Fine Hall when it went up in 1931 and Jones Hall now, where Paul Dirac spent the academic year 1934 to 1935, where Eugene Wigner held his joint appointment, where John von Neumann lectured, and where the Institute for Advanced Study kept its first borrowed rooms. Witten never works in it, but the building marks the address the physics he is learning came from.
suggested_refs: Old Fine Hall, now Jones Hall, Princeton, first home of the Institute for Advanced Study

stops.name: Princeton, the doctorate under David Gross
stops.date_confidence: 1976 attested for the degree; the month is conventional
stops.campa: The dissertation is titled Some Problems in the Short Distance Analysis of Gauge Theories, and it is passed in 1976, three years after he arrived in a department he had no training for. David Gross, who supervised it, will take a Nobel Prize in 2004 for asymptotic freedom, a property of the same gauge theories the thesis analyses. Witten is twenty-four. Everything he is known for is still ahead of him, and the history degree from Brandeis is now a curiosity in his file.
suggested_refs: Edward Witten, Some Problems in the Short Distance Analysis of Gauge Theories (Princeton PhD dissertation, 1976)

segments.name: Cambridge, Oxford, and the Society of Fellows

stops.name: Harvard University, the postdoctoral year
stops.date_confidence: 1976 attested for the start of the fellowship; the month is conventional
stops.campa: A postdoctoral fellowship takes him to Harvard, in Cambridge, where the field is finishing the standard model and has settled nothing about what comes after it. He is twenty-five and he publishes fast. Within five years he will have produced a proof of a theorem in general relativity that the relativists could not prove for themselves, and mathematicians will begin reading a physicist's papers as though they were mathematics, which is not a habit the two trades had kept.
suggested_refs: Harvard physics department, 1976 to 1977

stops.name: Oxford, the year across the water
stops.date_confidence: 1977 attested for the visit, the geography lens extending it to 1978; the month is defaulted and the departmental coordinate came from the gathering pass and was not independently checked
stops.campa: He crosses to Oxford for a year in the middle of the Harvard fellowship. English mathematical physics in the late seventies is Michael Atiyah's Oxford: index theorems, instantons, the gauge fields of Yang and Mills read as connections on bundles, a set of ideas the physicists and the geometers are only then finding they hold in common. Thirteen years later Atiyah will write, or Ludwig Faddeev will, the citation that hands Witten the Fields Medal. The sources disagree about which of them wrote it.
suggested_refs: The Oxford school of mathematical physics under Michael Atiyah in the late 1970s

stops.name: Harvard Society of Fellows, three years without duties
stops.date_confidence: 1977 to 1980 attested for the Junior Fellowship; the month is conventional
stops.campa: The Harvard Society of Fellows elects him a Junior Fellow: three years of income, dinners, and no teaching, no thesis, no supervisor, no requirement to produce anything at all. It is the appointment designed for a man who works best by wandering across problems, and he uses it exactly so. The fields he touches in this stretch do not stay separate afterwards. When the fellowship ends in 1980 Princeton offers him a faculty position and he goes back to the department that trained him.
stops.quote: It was clear that if I didn't spend the rest of my life concentrating on string theory, I would simply be missing my life's calling.
stops.quote_source: John Horgan, The End of Science (1996), as reproduced on Wikiquote; spoken long after these years and about a decision he reached in the following decade. The book itself was not fetched.
suggested_refs: The Harvard Society of Fellows, Junior Fellowship 1977 to 1980

stops.name: Cambridge, the marriage to Chiara Nappi
stops.date_confidence: 1979 attested for the marriage; the ceremony's location is sourced nowhere. Cambridge is a placeholder because both were at Harvard that year, and it replaces the gathering pass's Princeton, which is anachronistic. The month is defaulted
stops.campa: He marries Chiara Nappi, a theoretical physicist, who will hold a professorship at Princeton in her own right. Where the ceremony was held is nowhere written. Both of them are in Cambridge that year, so Cambridge is the placeholder and nothing more. Three children will come: Ilana, who becomes a neuroscientist at Princeton, Daniela, who becomes a biostatistician and takes an endowed chair at Washington, and Rafael, whose own path the record does not follow.
suggested_refs: Chiara Nappi's own publications in theoretical physics, and her later Princeton professorship

stops.name: Jadwin Hall, joining the Princeton faculty
stops.date_confidence: September 1980 attested in MacTutor; the day is not given
stops.campa: He returns to Princeton in September as a member of the physics faculty and rises to full professor inside the decade. The department is the one where Niels Bohr and John Wheeler worked out the mechanics of uranium fission in January 1939, in the weeks before they carried it to Washington. The war that came of it is forty years gone. Witten works on supersymmetry, on index theorems, on the quantity now called the Witten index, and the mathematics keeps growing under what he means as physics.
suggested_refs: Jadwin Hall, the Princeton physics department building occupied since 1970

stops.name: Princeton, a simple proof of the positive energy theorem
stops.date_confidence: 1981 attested for the paper in Communications in Mathematical Physics 80, 381 to 402; the month is defaulted. The gathering pass gave the title as A New Proof, which the INSPIRE record contradicts
stops.campa: He publishes a proof that the total energy of a gravitating system in general relativity cannot be negative, a statement relativists had believed for decades and could not establish. The proof uses spinors, which is to say it imports the machinery of quantum field theory into a problem of classical geometry, and it is a few pages of a method nobody in relativity had thought to try. The paper is called A Simple Proof of the Positive Energy Theorem. The mathematicians begin reading him.
suggested_refs: Edward Witten, A Simple Proof of the Positive Energy Theorem, Commun. Math. Phys. 80 (1981) 381-402

stops.name: Princeton, supersymmetry read as Morse theory
stops.date_confidence: 1982 attested for the paper; the month is defaulted
stops.campa: Supersymmetry and Morse Theory takes a supersymmetric quantum mechanics, deforms it by a function on a manifold, and recovers from the ground states of the deformed theory the Morse inequalities of differential topology. It is a physics paper that proves nothing new in physics and reproves something known in mathematics by a route no mathematician had taken. From here the direction of traffic is settled: he will keep using quantum field theory as an instrument for looking at geometry.
suggested_refs: Edward Witten, Supersymmetry and Morse Theory (1982)

stops.name: Princeton, the MacArthur Fellowship
stops.date_confidence: 1982 attested; the MacArthur has no ceremony and no venue, so the pin is only the town he was living in, and the month is conventional
stops.campa: The MacArthur Foundation gives him one of its fellowships, the grant the newspapers call the genius award: five years of money, no report required, no project to complete. He is thirty. The citation goes to a young Princeton professor whose work the foundation cannot easily place in a single field, which is the accurate description. There is no ceremony and no venue, so the pin here is only Princeton, where he is living and working while the money arrives.
suggested_refs: MacArthur Foundation fellowship class of 1982

stops.name: Bern, the Albert Einstein Medal
stops.date_confidence: 1985 attested for the award; the ceremony city is not sourced and Bern stands here as the seat of the Albert Einstein Society, not as a confirmed venue. The month is defaulted
stops.campa: The Albert Einstein Society, which keeps the apartment at Kramgasse 49 in Bern where Einstein wrote the papers of 1905, gives him its medal. Einstein was a patent clerk with no university post when he wrote them. Where Witten's ceremony was held is not recorded, so the pin is the society's own city. He is thirty-three. It is the first honour to reach him under Einstein's name, and a second, the Albert Einstein World Award of Science, will reach him in Riga thirty-one years later.
suggested_refs: The Albert Einstein Society, Kramgasse 49, Bern

stops.name: Trieste, the Dirac Medal of the ICTP
stops.date_confidence: 1985 attested; the month is conventional
stops.campa: The International Centre for Theoretical Physics at Trieste, founded by Abdus Salam on the Adriatic to keep physicists of the poorer countries inside the discipline, awards him the Dirac Medal. The medal carries the name of the man who spent the academic year 1934 in the Princeton building Witten's own department had left behind before he ever arrived there. Two honours reach him in this one year, the Einstein medal and this, and he is thirty-three years old.
suggested_refs: The ICTP Dirac Medal, Miramare, Trieste

segments.name: Fuld Hall, and the Medal No Physicist Had Won

stops.name: Fuld Hall, joining the Institute for Advanced Study
stops.date_confidence: 1987 attested for the appointment to the School of Natural Sciences; the month is defaulted. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Fuld Hall pin, inherited byte-identical from robert_oppenheimer.journey.json, and sits about 200 metres from the building's true position
stops.campa: He takes a permanent professorship at the Institute for Advanced Study, a few miles from the Princeton department, in the wooded campus with no students and no curriculum where Albert Einstein and John von Neumann sat among the founding six, where Robert Oppenheimer presided as director for twenty years, and where Claude Shannon spent a fellowship year in 1940 before the war redirected every mathematician in the building. Witten arrives in 1987 and does not leave. He is thirty-five.
stops.quote: It is very possible that a proper understanding of string theory will make the space-time continuum melt away.... String theory is a miracle through and through.
stops.quote_source: K.C. Cole, 'A Theory of Everything,' New York Times Magazine, 18 October 1987, as reproduced on Wikiquote. The magazine issue itself was not fetched.
suggested_refs: Fuld Hall, Institute for Advanced Study, and the roster of its founding professors

stops.name: The Institute, naming topological quantum field theory
stops.date_confidence: 1988 attested for the coinage of the term; the month is defaulted
stops.campa: He gives a name to a class of theories in which the observables do not depend on the metric of spacetime at all, only on its shape: topological quantum field theory. A physics with no distances and no clocks is a strange object for a physicist to want. What it computes are invariants of manifolds, the things topologists had been calculating by other means for sixty years, and it computes them by writing down an integral over all fields and evaluating it. The term sticks.
suggested_refs: Edward Witten, Topological Quantum Field Theory, Commun. Math. Phys. 117 (1988)

stops.name: The Institute, the Jones polynomial out of a path integral
stops.date_confidence: 1989 attested; the month is defaulted
stops.campa: Vaughan Jones had found, in an operator algebra, a polynomial that distinguishes knots. Witten shows it falls out of Chern-Simons theory: take the space of connections on a three-manifold, integrate over all of them with Richard Feynman's path integral, weight by the Chern-Simons action, and the expectation value of a Wilson loop around a knot is the Jones polynomial. Feynman built that integral as Wheeler's student at Princeton in the early forties, a mile from where this is written.
suggested_refs: Edward Witten, Quantum Field Theory and the Jones Polynomial, Commun. Math. Phys. 121 (1989)

stops.name: Kyoto, the Fields Medal
stops.date_confidence: August 1990 attested for the Congress and the award; the day is not fixed. The pin is the atlas's canonical Kyoto node inherited from richard_feynman.journey.json, not the Takaragaike conference centre at 35.0611, 135.7831 where the Congress actually sat
stops.campa: The International Congress of Mathematicians meets at Kyoto and gives him the Fields Medal, which no physicist had been given before him and none has been given since. The citation calls him definitely a physicist whose command of mathematics rivals few mathematicians, a sentence written to explain why a medal for mathematics is going to a man who has never published a paper mathematicians would call purely his own field. He is thirty-eight, and the prize marks the first time string theory's methods are honored by a body that owes it nothing.
stops.quote: Although he is definitely a physicist (as his list of publications clearly shows) his command of mathematics is rivaled by few mathematicians, and his ability to interpret physical ideas in mathematical form is quite unique.
stops.quote_source: Fields Medal citation for Edward Witten, International Congress of Mathematicians, Kyoto, 1990, as excerpted on Wikipedia. The research pool attributes the citation to Michael Atiyah in one place and to Ludwig Faddeev in another; the ICM Proceedings were not reached and the contradiction is left open.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Kyoto 1990, and the Fields Medal citation for Witten

stops.name: Mount Scopus, the honorary degree from the Hebrew University
stops.date_confidence: 1993 attested in MacTutor's honorary-degree list, correcting the gathering pass, which called the year a gap; the month is defaulted and the campus is a reconstruction, since no source says which campus conferred it
stops.campa: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem gives him an honorary doctorate. Which of its campuses conferred it is not stated, so the pin is Mount Scopus, the older hill. It is one of a series: Brandeis, where he read history, honoured him in 1988; Columbia follows in 1996, the University of Southern California in 2004, Johns Hopkins and Harvard in 2005. The country he lived in for a year as a child, without any source recording where or when, now writes his name on a degree.
stops.quote: The essence of it is that physics is about concepts, wanting to understand the concepts, the principles by which the world works.
stops.quote_source: Superstrings: A Theory of Everything?, eds. P.C.W. Davies and Julian Brown (1992), as reproduced on Wikiquote; spoken the year before this stop, not at it. The compressed form circulating in the research pool has been replaced with the full sentence.
suggested_refs: MacTutor's list of Witten's honorary degrees, Brandeis 1988 through Harvard 2005

stops.name: The Institute, Seiberg-Witten theory
stops.date_confidence: 1994 attested; the month is defaulted
stops.campa: With Nathan Seiberg he writes down exact solutions for supersymmetric gauge theories with extended supersymmetry, and the equations that come out of it reach into four-manifold topology and cut the labour of Donaldson theory to a fraction. Mathematicians who have never read a physics paper start reading this one, and the equations acquire his name and Seiberg's. He does not carry mathematics into physics. He runs the traffic the other way and hands geometers instruments they did not have.
suggested_refs: The Seiberg-Witten equations and their effect on four-manifold topology

stops.name: University of Southern California, Strings 95 and the eleventh dimension
stops.date_confidence: March 1995 attested for the conference and the talk; the day is not given in the sources reached
stops.campa: At the Strings conference at the University of Southern California he stands up and proposes that the five superstring theories, which had looked like five rival candidates for a theory of everything, are five limits of one theory in eleven dimensions. He calls it M-theory and declines to say what the M stands for. The field turns around inside a year. The period that follows is called the second superstring revolution, and it is dated from this talk in Los Angeles in March.
stops.quote: String theory is extremely attractive because gravity is forced upon us.
stops.quote_source: Michio Kaku, Hyperspace: A Scientific Odyssey (1995), as reproduced on Wikiquote. The book itself was not fetched.
suggested_refs: The Strings '95 conference proceedings, University of Southern California, March 1995

stops.name: La Silla, a rock in the belt named for him
stops.date_confidence: 3 May 1997 attested as the discovery date of minor planet 11349; the date on which the object was actually named for Witten was not established in the sources reached
stops.campa: At La Silla, on a ridge in the Atacama where the sky is dry enough to see through almost every night, the Belgian astronomer Eric Elst photographs a three-kilometre rock in the Vesta family of the main belt. It is catalogued as 11349 and afterwards given his name. He is alive to hear it, which is the ordinary way with asteroids and the unusual way with monuments. Nothing else in the physical world is named for him: no statue, no bust, one small stone between Mars and Jupiter.
suggested_refs: Minor planet 11349 Witten, Vesta family, discovered at La Silla 3 May 1997
sources: Asteroid catalogue data via web search

stops.name: Santa Barbara, the Kavli Institute
stops.date_confidence: no date attested. The visits to the Kavli Institute are a reconstruction supplied outside the verified pool, with no source and no years attached; 1998 is a pure convention. The pin is inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: The Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at Santa Barbara runs programs that bring the field's whole population to one campus for months at a time, and he is a frequent visitor through the string-theory programs. No source reached names a year, so the date on this stop is a convention and nothing else. The same campus fills every August with the CRYPTO conference, where Whitfield Diffie is a fixture. The two men share a lawn and a set of dormitories and, on the record, nothing else.
stops.quote: Good wrong ideas are extremely scarce... and good wrong ideas that even remotely rival the majesty of string theory have never been seen.
stops.quote_source: John Horgan, The End of Science (1996), as reproduced on Wikiquote. The research pool's paraphrase has been replaced with the recorded wording.
suggested_refs: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics program archives, UC Santa Barbara

stops.name: Evanston, the Nemmers Prize in Mathematics
stops.date_confidence: 2000 attested; the month is defaulted
stops.campa: Northwestern gives him the Nemmers Prize in Mathematics, an award endowed to cover fields the Nobel does not. He is a physicist and this is the mathematics prize, which by now surprises nobody. He is forty-nine, thirteen years into the Institute, and the honours arrive at a rate of roughly one a year for the rest of his working life, from mathematical societies and physical societies in about equal measure, and from national academies in half a dozen countries.
suggested_refs: Frederic Esser Nemmers Prize in Mathematics, Northwestern University, 2000

stops.name: The White House, the National Medal of Science
stops.date_confidence: the medal is for the year 2002 and was presented on 6 November 2003 in the East Room; Wikipedia's 2002 and MacTutor's 2003 are the award year and the ceremony date, not a disagreement between sources
stops.campa: George W. Bush hands him the National Medal of Science in the East Room, the medal itself awarded for the year 2002 and presented a year late, which is why two dates circulate. It is the highest scientific honour the United States confers. The work being cited is a body of theory with no experiment behind it and none in prospect: no accelerator has ever produced a superstring, and the man receiving the medal has said so more plainly than his critics have.
stops.quote: String theory is an attempt at a deeper description of nature by thinking of an elementary particle not as a little point but as a little loop of vibrating string.
stops.quote_source: PBS NOVA, 'The Elegant Universe' companion site, interview with Edward Witten, published alongside the 2003 documentary.
suggested_refs: Remarks by the President at Presentation of the National Medals of Science and Technology, East Room, 6 November 2003

stops.name: The Institute, the Charles Simonyi Professorship
stops.date_confidence: 2005 attested for the creation of the chair out of Charles Simonyi's donation; the month is defaulted. The gathering pass dated this to 1987, which is the year of the IAS appointment and not of the chair
stops.campa: Charles Simonyi, who wrote the first version of Microsoft Word, gives the Institute twenty-five million dollars, and part of it endows a chair in mathematical physics. Witten, eighteen years a professor there since arriving at thirty-five in 1987, becomes the first Charles Simonyi Professor and has held the position since. The appointment came in 1987; the chair followed eighteen years later, in 2005, two separate events rather than one, and Witten's own tenure at the Institute runs unbroken across both.
stops.quote: If I take the theory as we have it now, literally, I would conclude that extra dimensions really exist. They're part of nature.
stops.quote_source: PBS NOVA, 'The Elegant Universe' companion site, interview with Edward Witten, published alongside the 2003 documentary.
suggested_refs: The Charles Simonyi Professorship of Mathematical Physics, Institute for Advanced Study, endowed 2005
sources: Institute for Advanced Study scholar page

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the Henri Poincare Prize
stops.date_confidence: 2006 attested for the prize; the host city of that year's International Congress on Mathematical Physics is reconstructed from general knowledge of the congress series and was not re-verified this session. The month is defaulted
stops.campa: The International Association of Mathematical Physics gives him the Henri Poincare Prize at its triennial congress. The host city that year is reconstructed rather than verified, and Rio de Janeiro is the reconstruction. Poincare, dead since 1912, worked the seam Witten has spent thirty years working: topology invented to answer a question in dynamics, dynamics answered by a question in topology, and neither discipline willing to say which of the two the result belongs to.
suggested_refs: International Congress on Mathematical Physics, 2006, and the Henri Poincare Prize roll

stops.name: Vatican City, the Pontifical Academy of Sciences
stops.date_confidence: 2006 attested for the appointment by Benedict XVI; no ceremony is recorded, so the pin is the Academy's seat and the month is conventional
stops.campa: Benedict XVI appoints him to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, the body the Holy See keeps for scientists of any faith or none. The appointment carries no duties beyond the occasional plenary session in the Casina Pio IV, in the Vatican gardens behind Saint Peter's. Witten is Jewish and a theorist of eleven dimensions. The church that tried Galileo over a claim about two of them puts his name on its rolls, and no ceremony is recorded anywhere in the reachable sources.
suggested_refs: Casina Pio IV, seat of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, Vatican Gardens

stops.name: Stockholm, the Crafoord Prize in Mathematics
stops.date_confidence: 2008 attested, the prize shared with Maxim Kontsevich; the month is defaulted. It is the Crafoord Prize in Mathematics, a separate award from the Crafoord Prize in Astronomy given the same year to Rashid Sunyaev, which the gathering pass had welded into one title
stops.campa: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awards him the Crafoord Prize in Mathematics, shared with Maxim Kontsevich, for contributions to mathematics inspired by modern theoretical physics. The Crafoord was endowed to cover the disciplines Alfred Nobel left out. In the same year the academy gives its astronomy prize to Rashid Sunyaev; the two are separate awards and the material handed to this pass had welded them into a single title. Witten is fifty-six.
suggested_refs: Crafoord Prize in Mathematics 2008, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

segments.name: Late Honors, and the Institute Still

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Lorentz Medal
stops.date_confidence: 2010 attested; the month is defaulted
stops.campa: The Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences gives him the Lorentz Medal, struck every four years for theoretical physics and named for Hendrik Lorentz, whose transformations Einstein inherited and reinterpreted. It is awarded in Amsterdam. Witten is fifty-nine and has been at the Institute twenty-three years. The prize is for theoretical physics rather than for mathematics, and his working life has spent thirty years crossing the line between the two. Two medals reach him this year.

stops.name: London, the Isaac Newton Medal
stops.date_confidence: 2010 attested; the month is conventional and the pin is the Institute of Physics in London rather than a confirmed ceremony venue
stops.campa: The Institute of Physics in London gives him its Isaac Newton Medal, an international award the institute had founded two years earlier. Newton wrote the equations of gravity that Einstein replaced and that Witten's proof of 1981 established a property of. The Guardian interviews him in July of the same year and asks what is still unknown. He answers in a sentence of fifteen words and declines to expand it. It is his second medal of the year, after Amsterdam.
stops.quote: We know a lot of things, but what we don't know is a lot more.

stops.campa: He returns to Kyoto for the Kyoto Prize in Basic Sciences, twenty-four years after the same city gave him the Fields Medal in August 1990. Claude Shannon took the first of these prizes here in 1985, flying out for one of the last public appearances of his life. The Inamori Foundation cites a body of work that has moved, over thirty years, from quantum field theory into knot theory and back, and that has never once been checked against an experiment.

stops.campa: The University of Pennsylvania makes him an honorary Doctor of Sciences at its commencement. He is seventy, and the string theory whose eleven-dimensional limit he named is now old enough that the students in the audience were taught it as settled history rather than as a controversy. No accelerator has produced a string. The honorary degrees keep arriving anyway, and this one joins Brandeis, the Hebrew University, Columbia, Southern California, Johns Hopkins and Harvard.

stops.campa: He is still at the Institute, in the wooded campus he joined at thirty-five, now Professor Emeritus and still publishing. Einstein walked these lawns, Godel walked beside him, Oppenheimer ran the place for twenty years, and the buildings have not changed. There is no tomb to record and no death to date. The whole of his afterlife so far consists of prizes, an asteroid, and a reputation built on a theory no experiment has yet reached. He is in his seventies.
stops.quote: In my career I've only been able to take small jumps. Relatively small jumps.
